title: Breitbart and the Guardian Wrote the Same Science Story. That Doesn't Happen Often.
subtitle: A globally legible superlative erased outlet-level editorial identity
body_md:
Science sometimes produces a story with no partisan valence at all. The Tilcayo tiger cat, confirmed September 17 as the first new wild felid species named in over a century, appears to be one of them.

[Breitbart](https://www.breitbart.com/science/2026/09/17/scientists-discover-new-wild-cat-species-for-first-time-in-100-years/) ran: "A new wild cat species has been discovered for the first time in 100 years — the tilcayo tiger cat from the Bolivian Yungas." [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/17/new-cat-species-identified-bolivia) ran: "marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century." No ideological coloration. No divergent emphasis. The right-populist outlet and the left-liberal broadsheet reached for the same century-first framing because no other framing was available — the superlative was the story.

The LaBSE cosine similarity structure of this corpus is unusual. Thirteen outlets across eleven countries ran what amounts to a single story with minor variation. [Deutsche Welle](https://www.dw.com/en/bolivia-new-cat-species-discovered-by-scientists/a-79320205?maca=en-rss-en-all-1573-rdf) offered the standard formulation: "Genetic data confirmed that the small feline, called 'tilcayo' by locals, is a new species of cat. It's the first such discovery in more than 100 years." Nigeria's [The Punch](https://punchng.com/scientists-discover-new-wild-cat-species-after-100-years/?utm_source=rss.punchng.com&utm_medium=web) ran "Scientists have discovered the Tilcayo tiger cat in Bolivia, the first new wild cat species to be identified in more than 100 years." Canada, Spain, Singapore, Argentina — same story, same superlative, marginal variation in detail.

The genetic evidence is precise: the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats approximately 1.4 million years ago. The species was first brought to scientific attention by Bolivian biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose research was conducted in the Yungas cloud forests of Bolivia. One living specimen is currently known to exist.

Three deviations open slightly different windows on the same discovery. Spanish-language outlets foregrounded elements that anglophone coverage mostly passed over. [El País](https://elpais.com/ciencia/2026-09-18/el-tilcayo-primer-felino-salvaje-descubierto-en-mas-de-cien-anos.html) named and centered the scientist: "el linaje del pequeño animal, descrito por la científica Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz en los bosques nubosos de Bolivia, se separó del resto de los gatos tigre hace 1,4 millones de años." Argentina's [La Nación](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/new-cat-species-identified-bolivia-first-in-over-a-century) reported the rural origin story — that a field family noticed atypical behaviors in the animal after keeping it for a year before it entered the scientific record. [El Sol de Mexico](https://elpais.com/ciencia/2026-09-18/el-tilcayo-primer-felino-salvaje-descubierto-en-mas-de-cien-anos.html) named the prior baseline: the first feline species since the pampas cat was identified in 1923, anchoring the discovery against a specific historical predecessor.

[The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/new-cat-species-identified-in-bolivia-first-in-over-a-century/article71478144.ece) was the only outlet to introduce a note of scientific caution: "Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago; little is yet known about the biology and lifestyle." That hedge — the species is named but essentially unstudied — appeared nowhere else. Every other outlet carried the discovery as a completed scientific milestone. The Hindu treated it as the beginning of a research problem.

[Straits Times](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/new-cat-species-identified-bolivia-first-in-over-a-century) gave Southeast Asian readers the most grounded physical description, specifying the animal's dimensions: 46 centimetres long, 1.4 kilograms. Pakistan's Geo News published two separate articles on the same discovery — more volume than any other outlet in the corpus — a signal of readership interest that is hard to explain but impossible to miss.

The political lesson the Tilcayo corpus offers is modest but real. Editorial identity — which ordinarily bends every story through a partisan lens, assigning heroes and villains, winners and losers — has a clear boundary. A first-in-a-century taxonomic finding from a Bolivian cloud forest, with no geopolitical vector, no domestic policy implication, and no identifiable adversary, lands the same way in Breitbart and the Guardian. The story's neutrality was its own kind of editorial event.
